newsitem.title: USA: Oregon developing new wheat strain for Asia market.
newsitem.headline: Oregon developing new wheat strain for Asia market.

text.p: Guotran Hou picked up a noodle and inspected it like a picky shopper going through a basket of less-than-perfect tomatoes.
"You don't want it like this," said Hou, an Asian food specialist at the Wheat Marketing Center here. "Too dark. It doesn't look good."
Rosie Dellumes, a research and development manager at Robin Hood Manufacturing in the Philippines who was visiting recently, agreed.
"Nobody likes dark noodles," she said. "We need brighter noodles, and texture is very important. The noodles should be firm and ... of very good texture."
Hou is all too aware of that. He and others at the center are working feverishly to develop a tougher noodle made from Northwest wheat to meet Asian demand.

To date, the key wheat crop in Oregon and neighboring states has been the soft white variety, which is used for cakes and biscuits. But Asian noodles, which require a firmer texture than noodles common to North America, are made from hard white wheat.
Hard white wheat is not grown in Oregon, but that may be changing.

In addition to Hou's work, the University of Oregon at Corvallis is experimenting with the hard white variety at its wheat growing station in Pendleton, Oregon's grain-producing area in the northeastern part of the state.

Researchers believe if the Pendleton station is successful in growing hard white wheat, farmers can be persuaded to switch to the new crop. A Hard White Wheat Review Conference has even been established, in conjunction with teams from six Asian countries, to move production along.
But competitors aren't waiting. Australia is a key producer of hard white wheat for the Asian market. Canada also exports this variety.

And the Asian market is important. Overall figures for U.S. wheat sales in the year ending in May 1997 show that half of the 26 million metric tons of wheat shipped out of the United States was sent to Asia.

Farmers in Washington, Idaho and Montana already have started to produce hard white wheat in response to Asian demand. Hou believes Oregon farmers will be able to commercially produce hard white wheat within five years.

On its recent visit to the Wheat Marketing Center, the team from the Philippines was discussing noodle needs with local food scientists. Dellumes' company produces a wet noodle that is usually cooked with vegetables and fish or meat. The noodles brew in the soup-based dish for about 30 minutes, so a firm texture is essential.

The group of four Filipino food specialists moved from the center's board room to its gleaming work area. When one visitor observed that the area looked like a kitchen for a fast-food restaurant, Hou made a correction.
"It isn't a kitchen," he said politely. "It is a food laboratory."

The periodic visits of Asian delegations to the center are important, as they help identify consumer preferences. A noodle's color, for example, is key. Noodles made of whole or darker wheats won't work in the region, because consumers want brighter noodles. Surprisingly, experts agree that good taste is not a noodle's most redeeming quality.

Boy Ng, a baking technician with U.S. Wheat Associates in Makati City, Philippines, said American wheat exporters traditionally have profited from the close political relationship the United States has with his country.

But consumers' tastes and preferences are starting to supersede politics. Hou notes that 10 years ago, American wheat exporters controlled 90 percent of the wheat market in South Korea, another Asian country with historically close U.S. ties. But that has dropped to 70 percent as Australian exporters have moved in with hard white wheat.
And even though the Northwest wheat efforts are taking off, competitors aren't sitting still.
"I think right now we are catching up with them," Hou said. "But we need to do more study and keep up our research to compete."
